rationale: B wins by being more surgically useful: "The AI answer box becomes a checkout counter" gives a reporter a sharper commerce frame than A's broader "Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon," which drags in competitors the update did not supply. B also finds a real extra data angle in "What 'hundreds of millions of queries a month' is worth to a publisher, exactly." The bill comes due on grounding: B's "starts paying publishers it was being sued over" is sloppy because the facts say legal threats, not lawsuits, but its proof gates are honest enough to keep the set ahead by a nose.
gaps_in_A: "for the first time, an AI search product is inserting itself into the transaction" is not supported by the update. Big categorical firsts need proof, not vibes.

"Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon" overreaches. Google and Amazon are plausible context, but neither appears in the supplied facts and no competitive response or share data is provided.
"publishers and their legal teams will need to respond publicly" assumes a reaction timeline the update does not establish.
"publisher participation appears opt-in; content is cited regardless" adds an inference inside the facts section. If it is an inference, label it as one; don't smuggle it in as evidence.
gaps_in_B: "Perplexity starts paying publishers it was being sued over" is wrong on the supplied facts. The update says criticism and legal threats, not active lawsuits.

"Perplexity is now paid twice on the same answer" asserts the answer before the reporting. The set later admits the angle dies if referral revenue is shared, which means the headline is too confident.
"the referral-fee pool apparently is not" is a useful suspicion, but still an inference. It belongs under the question to verify, not as the spine of a pitch until confirmed.
"first visible consumer-revenue mechanisms" is not in the update. Maybe true, maybe not; don't make a private-company revenue-history claim without sourcing it.
